content: The Slippery Elm, scientifically known as Ulmus rubra Muhl, is a species of elm tree native to eastern North America. Its range extends from southeastern North Dakota to southern Quebec, and southward to northern Florida and eastern Texas. While it resembles the American Elm in appearance, it is more closely related to the European Wych Elm due to similarities in flower structure. This species is less vulnerable to Dutch elm disease compared to many other elms and exhibits a distinct branching pattern. The heartwood of the tree is reddish-brown, which has earned it the alternative name Red Elm. Other common names include Gray Elm, Soft Elm, Moose Elm, and Indian Elm. The Slippery Elm is a deciduous tree that typically grows to a height of 10–20 meters, with a trunk diameter of up to 50 centimeters. Its leaves are 10–18 centimeters long, with a rough texture, a coarsely double-serrated margin, and an asymmetrical base. The tree produces flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge. These flowers grow in clusters of 10–20 and are very short-stalked. The fruit is an oval-shaped, winged samara approximately 2 centimeters long, containing a single seed at its center. The Slippery Elm can be distinguished from the American Elm by the hairiness of its buds and twigs, as opposed to the smooth buds and twigs of the American Elm. This tree thrives in moisture-rich uplands but can also grow in drier, intermediate soils. However, it is rarely cultivated outside the United States. Uses The Slippery Elm is a highly valuable tree with numerous applications. The inner bark can be ground into a nutrient-rich gruel, which is capable of sustaining an individual for a short period. This bark contains mucilage, a substance that is particularly effective in treating sore throats. The bark can be dried, ground into a powder, and used to make tea. Both the tea and the gruel are beneficial for soothing the digestive tract, making them useful for conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and gastritis. Since the bark primarily consists of mucilage and nutrients, it is not classified as a drug and has no known contraindications. Historically, the bark has also been used as an abortifacient. It was moistened with water and inserted into the cervix to induce abortion. This practice led to the implementation of elm stick laws in several U.S. states, which prohibited the sale of slippery elm bark in pieces longer than a certain length. Selling whole slippery elm bark is now banned in some countries, including the United Kingdom, due to this historical use. The fibrous inner bark is strong and durable, making it suitable for spinning into thread, twine, or rope. It has been used to create bowstrings, ropes, jewelry, clothing, snowshoe bindings, woven mats, and even components of musical instruments. The wood of the Slippery Elm is highly shock-resistant due to its interlocking grain, making it ideal for constructing wagon wheel hubs. It is also used for crafting bows, as it is both strong and flexible. Once cured, the wood is excellent for fire-starting using the bow drill method, as it produces a fine, flammable powder under friction. Cultivars There are no known cultivars of the Slippery Elm. Hybrid Cultivars In the 1960s, Ulmus rubra was used as a hybrid parent, resulting in the development of cultivars such as Coolshade, Lincoln, Rosehill, and possibly Willis. In later years, it was also utilized in the Wisconsin breeding program to produce hybrids named Repura and Revera, although neither of these appears to have been commercially released as of 2007. Arboreta and Accessions The Slippery Elm is part of several arboreta and botanical collections worldwide.
